incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of artificial intelligence scammers who are using deepfake videos and fake social media profiles featuring his likeness to defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals create fake accounts across multiple platforms and produce AI-generated videos offering immigration services that Leal has never provided, typically requesting payments of thousands of dollars through apps like Venmo, Zelle, and Cash App for services such as obtaining US residency or securing release from detention centers. The scheme escalated dramatically in recent months after Leal's office first noticed suspicious activity in October.

To combat the fraud, Leal hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scammers typically direct victims through social media videos to contact phone numbers via WhatsApp, where they exchange fake contracts and phony testimonials. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the source of the scams. He warns immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to avoid those requesting immediate payments through digital money transfer apps.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake article featuring a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has surfaced online, exemplifying a rising wave of AI-generated investment scams. The fictional piece depicted the two engaging in heated debate over Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform that Australian authorities warn against. The interview never occurred, yet such deceptive content is becoming increasingly common and sophisticated as artificial intelligence technology advances.

Australian securities regulator ASIC reports that investment scams have surged dramatically, with the watchdog removing 19,400 schemes last year, representing a 182 percent increase. The regulator identified a 279 percent jump in phishing scam takedowns and a 151 percent rise in fake investment platform removals. Scammers commonly impersonate prominent Australians including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart, creating elaborate webs of fake websites, articles, and testimonials. ASIC urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services license numbers and avoid investment opportunities that seem too good to be true.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A class-action lawsuit has been filed against Oura, the smart ring company valued at $11 billion, by the Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco. The suit alleges that Oura made false advertising claims about its sleep tracking accuracy. The company marketed rings priced at $300 and up by claiming they could detect sleep stages with 95% accuracy comparable to hospital sleep labs. However, the lawsuit contends that Oura's sensors and algorithms cannot actually measure the physiological signals needed for accurate sleep stage detection and instead rely on "AI-generated guesses" no better than random chance.

Oura disputes the allegations, stating that it stands behind its science and research with peer-reviewed studies validating its sleep staging against clinical standards. The company notes that while its rings estimate sleep stages using heart rate, movement, and temperature data, they are not medical devices meant to replace clinical sleep studies. It remains unclear at this early stage whether Oura Ring customers could join the lawsuit or what compensation might result from a trial or settlement. This lawsuit follows a previous class-action case against Oura involving claims that the company collected personal information without customer consent over a two-year period.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments. The group operated across multiple countries and ran a data leak site. Researchers found that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten target organizations between April 8 and May 21, 2026. The ESXi ransomware encrypts virtual machine files using ChaCha20 encryption while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. A custom tool called esxi_finder.py was used to scan for and identify ESXi hosts and vCenter servers within victim networks.

Investigators identified a second cluster of Aurora activity with medium confidence, affecting eight organizations across six countries. This group used different tactics, including exploiting SQL Server commands, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration to self-hosted S3 storage. The research revealed that Aurora operators imposed strict operational restrictions on the AI agent, prohibiting DCSync attacks, account lockouts, and adding new computer objects to domains, suggesting a disciplined approach to avoiding detection and maintaining network stability during attacks.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
A major Pizza Hut franchisee filed a lawsuit in Texas alleging that the chain's new AI-powered delivery system, called Dragontail, caused over $100 million in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across the Northeast, claims the system created operational problems by giving DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen operations. This visibility allegedly allowed drivers to wait up to 15 minutes for multiple orders rather than delivering pizzas immediately, resulting in cold, late arrivals and reduced customer satisfaction. The franchisee also claims drivers could see tip amounts and payment methods, leading some to reject certain deliveries.

Before Dragontail's 2024 rollout, Chaac's restaurants had over 90 percent on-time deliveries and strong sales growth. After implementation, the company experienced severe performance drops, with New York City sales declining from positive 10.19 percent to negative 9.78 percent year-over-year. Chaac alleges Pizza Hut failed to provide adequate training or support and ignored complaints as metrics worsened. The franchisee is seeking more than $100 million in damages plus attorney fees. Pizza Hut stated it is reviewing the lawsuit claims and will respond through legal channels. This lawsuit comes as Pizza Hut's parent company plans to close 250 U.S. locations.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Fraudsters are running a sophisticated scam targeting Hollywood figures by impersonating famous podcasters and their representatives. Broadway performer Seth Rudetsky received a fake invitation from Nikki Glaser's podcast offering $4,000 to $5,000, complete with personalized details about his career that appeared authentic. Similarly, comedian Bruce Vilanch believed Terry Gross from NPR's Fresh Air wanted him as a guest. The scammers used AI-generated emails with impressive specificity and knowledge of the targets' work, making the invitations seem legitimate and establishing credibility through detailed correspondence.

The scams took different forms. Vilanch was eventually asked to send money to help NPR with funding issues before the fake interview occurred, and when he joined a video call, a stranger claiming to be Mike conducted it instead of Gross. Rudetsky was guided through Facebook permission settings and lost control of his social media account. Both men were initially fooled by the personalized approach and the apparent effort the scammers invested. Rudetsky continues receiving fraudulent podcast invitations from other celebrities and now sometimes engages the scammers to test their tactics. The scammers show no signs of stopping their operations.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
A fake American think tank funded by Israel published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days, designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots to make pro-Israel arguments. The website, registered under the nonexistent Hanover Institute for Public Policy, presented Israel's positions on topics including Palestinian torture, war crimes, and Gaza starvation as neutral academic research. The site was built on a platform specifically engineered for generative engine optimization, allowing it to manipulate how chatbots cite sources and frame responses. The New York production company Piro Inc filed the operation as Israeli government propaganda under federal foreign agent registration law.

The campaign is part of a broader Israeli effort spending tens of millions of dollars through intermediaries like the European advertising group Havas Media to manipulate AI systems. Israeli officials have expressed frustration that the spending has failed, with public opinion polls showing Americans increasingly sympathetic to Palestinians and critical of Israeli military actions. Researchers warn that this type of AI manipulation represents a growing threat, as poisoned training data can influence chatbot responses without transparent sourcing, making fact-checking impossible for users.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have sued two popular AI music generators named Udio and Suno. The labels accuse both companies of illegally copying thousands of copyrighted songs to train their AI models without permission or payment. The lawsuits claim the companies have deliberately hidden what music they used for training, which would reveal massive copyright infringement. The record labels filed separate lawsuits against Udio in New York and Suno in Massachusetts.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate famous songs by using the AI generators with specific prompts. For example, they generated songs resembling works by The Beatles, Chuck Berry, Mariah Carey, and Green Day. The labels submitted a lengthy list of thousands of copyrighted recordings they believe were scraped, along with a thumb drive containing AI-generated music they claim directly copies original works. Both companies previously claimed their training practices constitute fair use, but the labels dispute this assertion, setting up a significant legal battle over how generative AI services can use existing creative work.

incidents.title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio
incidents.summary:
Universal Music Group has reached a settlement with AI music startup Udio, ending a lawsuit that accused the company of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. Under the agreement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that only uses authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, stream and share songs. UMG chairman Lucian Grainge stated the settlement demonstrates the company's commitment to supporting artists and songwriters while embracing new technologies and business models. The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

The lawsuit originated when UMG and other major record labels accused Udio of illegally training its AI on copyrighted music. The lawsuit specifically cited The Temptations' hit "My Girl," claiming Udio's system generated a similar song called "Sunshine Melody" with matching melodies, chords and backing vocals. Udio's CEO Andrew Sanchez expressed enthusiasm about collaborating with UMG, stating the partnership will help redefine how AI supports artists and fans. This represents Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label, and artists on the new platform will be compensated for their participation.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers in a Los Angeles lawsuit apologized for using artificial intelligence to prepare legal filings that contained fabricated case citations, fake quotes, and nonexistent legal holdings. The lawsuit involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, a homeowner whose Carson home was damaged by fire in 2020 and then flooded during repairs. After allegedly experiencing delays in getting State Farm's approval for repairs, the work was never completed, leading Meni-Siliga and her husband to drain their savings, declare bankruptcy, and lose their home to foreclosure. Attorney Jacquelene Robinson admitted that seven case citations across eight filings did not actually exist, and she used an AI tool called Irys that she mistakenly believed performed accuracy checks.

The incident highlights a growing problem in the legal industry, where 41 percent of law firms now use generative AI. A Paris-based researcher's database has identified 1,922 cases of legal hallucinations worldwide, mostly in the United States. Last year, a California attorney received a record $10,000 fine for using ChatGPT in a brief containing 21 fabricated quotes. The case involving State Farm is scheduled to go to trial in October.

stories.Headline: Datametrex Plans to Focus on AI, Data Centre, and Patent Licensing
stories.Summary:
Datametrex AI Limited announced plans to shut down its healthcare operations to focus on artificial intelligence, data centre technology, and patent licensing. The company operates medical clinics in Edmonton, Calgary, and Vancouver, British Columbia, providing primary and emergency care services. The gradual wind-down aims to streamline the corporate structure, reduce operating costs and regulatory requirements, and improve financial performance by redirecting resources toward core business areas.

The company will manage the transition carefully, considering operational, financial, contractual, and regulatory factors. Management plans to assess opportunities to maximize value from healthcare assets during the process. The strategic shift allows Datametrex to concentrate capital and resources on artificial intelligence and data centre initiatives, which align with long-term objectives. The company indicated it would provide further updates as developments occur.

stories.Headline: Pakistan and Saudi Arabia Extend Partnership in AI and Data
stories.Summary:
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have agreed to deepen their cooperation in artificial intelligence, data governance, and emerging technologies. The agreement was announced following a meeting between Pakistan's Federal Minister for Information Technology and Telecommunication Shaza Fatima Khawaja and Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority President Abdullah bin Sharaf Alghamdi at the LEAP 2026 conference in Riyadh. The two nations plan to establish a comprehensive and long-term technology partnership.

During the discussion, Pakistan's minister outlined the country's national AI and data governance initiatives while reaffirming Pakistan's commitment to building a strong data ecosystem and growing its digital economy. Both countries intend to collaborate on emerging technologies and create a lasting framework for cooperation. The partnership reflects a broader regional focus on advancing artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure, technology skills, and data-driven development.

stories.Headline: FG, IFAD, stakeholders push AI-enabled extension to transform Nigeria's agriculture
stories.Summary:
# Summary

The Federal Government, International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), and other organizations are working to introduce artificial intelligence-powered digital extension services to help Nigerian farmers. At a workshop in Abuja, stakeholders committed to using this technology to deliver timely agricultural advice tailored to individual farmers' locations, crops, weather conditions, and market opportunities. The IFAD country director emphasized that AI-enabled extension is crucial for transforming Nigeria's agricultural policies into practical services that improve food security and support climate resilience.

The initiative addresses a critical shortage of agricultural extension workers in Nigeria, where the ratio of one extension agent to between 5,000 and 10,000 farmers far exceeds the recommended benchmark of one agent per 800 to 1,000 farmers. A pilot program in Kano and Ogun States has already registered nearly 21,000 farmers through the FarmerChat AI platform, which provides weather updates and pest guidance in multiple languages. However, challenges including limited smartphone ownership, internet connectivity issues, and low digital literacy must be addressed for wider adoption.

stories.Headline: Brazil's electoral court sets new standards for AI deepfakes after case involving Sen. Bolsonaro
stories.Summary:
Brazil's electoral court established new standards for identifying artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes in political advertising as the country prepares for October elections. The ruling came from a case involving opposition candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who displayed AI-generated images of his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, at his party's convention in July. The court voted 4-3 to not punish Bolsonaro, determining the deepfake was used at a private event before his official candidacy announcement rather than as a public political advertisement.

In a separate 5-2 vote, the court defined political deepfakes as synthetic content created through artificial intelligence that realistically reproduces the image, voice, or speech of any person. These new standards will govern the vast amount of online campaign content from candidates leading up to the first round of voting on October 4. Broadcasters must allocate significant airtime for candidate advertisements, including 14 minutes daily for nearly 1,000 thirty-second ads.

stories.Headline: Protein Industries Canada invests in AI technology to boost on-farm productivity and bring new solutions to farmers
stories.Summary:
Protein Industries Canada is investing $4.9 million into two artificial intelligence projects designed to help Canadian farmers increase productivity and improve safety. The projects involve partnerships between companies like TerraVision360, Metos Canada, Rocky Mountain Equipment, Super GeoAI Technology Inc., and Southview Farms. The first project will create an AI tool to predict and manage disease risk in pulse crops by analyzing weather and crop data, enabling farmers to apply fungicides more strategically and reduce costs. The second project will develop a drone and LiDAR system to measure grain volumes in storage bins accurately while eliminating the need for dangerous manual climbing.

These investments are part of Canada's effort to advance agricultural innovation and support the adoption of made-in-Canada AI solutions. Government officials emphasized that the projects will strengthen farm competitiveness, reduce operational risks, and enhance worker safety across the agriculture sector. The funding comes through the Pan-Canadian Artificial Intelligence Strategy and supports the broader goal of growing Canada's plant-based food and ingredient industry to $25 billion.

Prasada emphasized that the international recognition reflects growing confidence in India's IT foundation and emerging startup ecosystem. He reiterated India's openness to strategic partnerships with global technology leaders as the country works to shape the future of innovation and lead the next wave of the global technology revolution.

stories.Headline: USF Faculty Split on AI Use in Classrooms
stories.Summary:
University of South Florida held a panel discussion Monday where faculty members debated whether artificial intelligence should be embraced, adapted to, or resisted in classroom settings. John Licato, an associate professor in the Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, and Stephanie Arthur, an assistant professor in the College of Education, both support using AI tools. They argue that AI is already present in students' lives and can help with personalized learning and language support. Licato noted that AI can save students time and money on projects, while Arthur emphasized the importance of building AI literacy early, even starting with first graders.

Deepak Singh, a writing instructor at the Judy Genshaft Honors College, disagreed strongly. He believes AI undermines human creativity and intelligence, arguing that students should create work through their own effort rather than relying on machines. Singh also contends that students who learn without AI assistance retain more information. The faculty acknowledged that some concerns exist, including the potential for AI to replace meaningful human interaction and feedback necessary for learning.
